summary: For ages 10-11, this capstone strand builds precise mathematical vocabulary and notation: distinguishing an expression (no equals sign; it can be evaluated or simplified but not solved) from an equation (asserts two things are equal; an equation such as 3x + 5 = 11 can be solved) from a formula (a special kind of equation that states a general rule relating quantities); naming circle parts correctly (radius = centre to circumference, diameter = all the way across through the centre = 2 × radius, circumference = the distance around); and attaching the right units to a quantity (volume in cm³, distinct from area in cm²). Following EEF, learners should read expressions as descriptions of relationships, not just instructions to calculate, and use terms that reflect mathematical structure.
misconceptions: Conflates expression, equation and formula — calls 3x + 5 an equation, or uses the terms interchangeably
Confuses circle parts — says the diameter is centre-to-edge (that is the radius), or calls the circumference the 'edge'/'side'
Omits the volume unit or uses the wrong dimension — '60' or '60 cm²' instead of '60 cm³'
Reads an algebraic expression only as an instruction to calculate rather than a relationship, mishandling order of operations

activities.title: Sort algebra cards by the role of '='
steps: Sort three cards — '3x + 5', '3x + 5 = 11', 'V = l × w × h' — into three bins labelled expression, equation and formula.

For each card, say out loud what makes it belong there: Does it have an equals sign? If it does, is it a statement of equality that is true only for particular values of an unknown (one you solve), or a general rule relating quantities that holds for any values (a formula, which is a special kind of equation)?

Explain the consequence: an expression can be evaluated (worked out once you know the value of the letter) or simplified, but not solved, while an equation like 3x + 5 = 11 can be solved (find the unknown that makes it true).
Test the boundary with a non-example question such as 'Is 3x + 5 an equation? Why not?' and 'What single change would turn 3x + 5 into an equation?'
activities.insight: The presence and role of '=' is the defining feature: an expression has none, an equation like 3x + 5 = 11 asserts equality for a particular unknown value (and can be solved), and a formula is a special kind of equation that states a general rule relating quantities for any values. The precise term changes what you are allowed to do with the object.

activities.title: Build the radius–diameter–circumference relationship on a circle
steps: On a labelled circle, point to and name the radius, the diameter and the circumference in your own words.
State how the radius and diameter are related and justify it: the diameter goes all the way across through the centre and is exactly twice the radius.
Using a drawn or physical circle, mark a radius, then mark the diameter as two radii end-to-end through the centre, then trace the full distance around for the circumference.

Catch a deliberate error: respond to 'the diameter is the distance from the centre to the edge' by correcting it (that is the radius) and explaining what difference the correction makes to any calculation.
activities.insight: Radius, diameter and circumference name distinct features that stand in a fixed relationship (diameter = 2 × radius), so the words are not interchangeable; swapping radius and diameter gives a wrong answer. For a length such as the circumference it halves or doubles the answer, and for an area it multiplies or divides the answer by 4.

activities.title: Attach the right unit to volume
steps: Work out the volume of a box (e.g. with a unit-cube model, counting how many 1 cm cubes fill it) and write the answer with its unit.
State why the unit is cm³ and not cm² or a bare number: volume fills space in three dimensions, so it is counted in cubic units.
Contrast a volume (cm³) with an area (cm²) for the same figure, saying what each measures.
activities.insight: A quantity is incomplete without its unit, and the unit must match the dimension: volume fills space so it is measured in cubic units (cm³), distinct from area's square units (cm²).

activities.title: Expert dialogue: justify the precise term
steps: Respond to an in-role questioner who insists on the exact term: 'Is that an expression or an equation? What makes it one?'
When you use loose language, restate it in precise mathematical terms when asked.
Defend your classification or your circle-part naming with the defining feature, not just the answer.
activities.insight: Being able to name the defining reason — the role of the equals sign, centre-to-edge versus all-the-way-across — is what distinguishes precise understanding from loose usage.

checkQuestion: A child said '3x + 5 is an equation', and 'the diameter is the distance from the centre to the edge of a circle.' Are these right? Fix them, and explain the difference each correction makes.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for '3x + 5 is an EXPRESSION' (it has no equals sign; an equation asserts equality like 3x+5=11, and a formula is a general rule like V=l×w×h) and 'the distance from the centre to the edge is the RADIUS; the diameter goes all the way across through the centre and is twice the radius'; and for why it matters (you can solve an equation but only evaluate an expression; confusing radius and diameter halves or doubles the answer). Surfaced for discussion, not scored.
